The bill would let the Secretary of the Department of Health appoint a wider range of people as authorised officers to enforce the Tobacco Plain Packaging Act.

Currently only federal public servants and Australian Federal Police members can be appointed; the bill would add people employed by other Commonwealth entities, state or territory health or police officers, and local government officials with health or tobacco enforcement duties.

The change is designed to handle future organisational changes, such as the National Measurement Institute restructuring, and to allow local officers to respond to non-compliance in remote areas, but only with the agreement of the relevant state or territory.
Expands the categories of persons eligible to be appointed as authorised officers under the Act.
Allows state and territory police officers and local government officials to be appointed with the consent of their jurisdiction.
Responds to potential future organisational changes, such as the National Measurement Institute altering its employment arrangements.

The Department of Health, the National Measurement Institute, state and territory health departments, state and territory police, and local government officials with health or tobacco enforcement responsibilities.

The majority voted against an amendment to the usual [second reading motion](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html), which is "*That this bill be now read a second time*" (or in plain English, "*that the House agree with the main idea of the bill*"). Instead, Labor Senator [Catherine King](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/ballarat/catherine_king) moved the following: > *That all words after "That" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > *"whilst not declining to give the bill a second reading, the House:* > *(1) notes that progress on lowering smoking rates has stalled following the Government's cuts to tobacco control measures; and* > *(2) calls on the Government to re-invest in lowering smoking rates."*

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2018-09-18.6.2) to agree with the bill's main idea. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill for a [second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ### Bill's main idea The [bill was introduced](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6155) "*to expand the range of persons who can be appointed as authorised officers for the purposes of undertaking compliance and enforcement activities under the [Tobacco Plain Packaging Act 2011]*". Read more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1819a/19bd025).
Tobacco Plain Packaging Amendment Bill 2018 - in Committee - Require manufacturer consent for plain packaging

The speaker supported the Tobacco Plain Packaging Amendment Bill 2018 as a minor technical change, but criticised the government for stalled progress on smoking reduction, noting no national anti-smoking campaigns since 2012 and cuts to Indigenous cessation programs, and called for renewed investment in tobacco control.

The member supported the Tobacco Plain Packaging Amendment Bill 2018 and expressed concern about high smoking rates among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, citing 39% daily smokers compared to 14% in the general population. He criticised the Abbott government for cutting $500 million from Indigenous programs, including $130 million from the tackling Indigenous smoking program, and argued that continued funding for anti-smoking initiatives is essential.

The speaker argued that progress on lowering smoking rates has stalled due to the government’s 2014 cuts to tobacco control measures and called for reinvestment in community-led programs, specifically highlighting the Deadly Choices program run by the Institute for Urban Indigenous Health in Brisbane.

The speaker supported the Tobacco Plain Packaging Amendment Bill 2018, noting that plain packaging contributed to a 12.8% reduction in tobacco consumption and calling for better funding of community-controlled health initiatives, while criticising the government’s stalled progress and the Nationals’ acceptance of $15,700 in tobacco donations.

The Tobacco Plain Packaging Amendment Bill 2018 expands the range of authorised officers for compliance activities under the Tobacco Plain Packaging Act 2011, aiming to reduce smoking prevalence and associated health, social and economic costs.
